Chapter 3: Shame, Stigma, and the Power of Naming.
Even as more stories are shared and voices grow stronger, there's still this heavy weight of shame and stigma that hangs around.
For so many generations, women have been taught to hide, to shrink themselves, and to say sorry for their bodies and their desires. These roots go deep—they're tangled up in our language, our traditions, and even our closest relationships.
Picture this: one woman remembers the first time she tried to talk about her body with a partner. She was nervous, didn’t know how to start, and the conversation just turned awkward. Right away, she felt herself pulling back, scared of being judged. The silence afterward? It was almost tangible—thick with all those unspoken fears. That moment made it clear that shame isn’t just something we carry alone; it’s shaped by how others respond.
Then there’s the story of someone raised in a strict religious home. She was taught from the start that her body was a source of temptation, something to hide and control. The rules were tough, and breaking them came with real consequences. Now, even as an adult, she finds it hard to shake the feeling that there’s something wrong with her body.
Some women have never even spoken the real word for their own anatomy. Instead, they use euphemisms or just avoid the topic altogether. One woman actually laughs as she remembers all the silly nicknames her family used—each one more ridiculous than the last. But underneath the laughter, there’s this sense of loss—the realization that language shapes how we see ourselves. Because if you can’t name something, how can you really understand it?
For others, shame is tied to physical changes—like aging, illness, or injury. One woman describes the shock of menopause, how it felt like her body was betraying her. Suddenly, she felt invisible, pushed aside in a culture that prizes youth above everything else. But as time went on, she started to see her body differently—she learned to value its strength, its resilience.
There are also stories of women carrying shame from trauma. One survivor of abuse talks about her long road to healing. For years, she felt cut off from her own body, almost like it belonged to someone else. Therapy helped, but what really made a difference was finding a community of other survivors. Together, they learned to name their experiences, to reclaim their bodies, and to let go of shame that never should have been theirs in the first place.
Here’s something powerful most people don’t realize: naming things changes everything. Just saying a word out loud can be transformative. It’s not just about language—it’s about taking ownership, about having the right to define your own experience. When women start naming their bodies, their desires, and even their pain, they’re taking back what was taken from them.
These stories show that shame grows in secrecy. But when women are encouraged to speak openly, that stigma, little by little, starts to fade. Sure, it’s not easy—old habits are hard to break, and the fear of being judged is very real. But with every story, every honest conversation, the walls begin to crumble. And that’s how real change begins.
